findings.title: Enrich signature changed from (int, error) to int, losing error propagation context
findings.description: The Enrich() method previously returned (int, error) with distinct errors (fetcher.ErrChallenge and ErrEnrichmentAborted) allowing callers to distinguish bot-protection challenges from generic failures. The new signature returns only int, forcing callers to rely solely on the enrichment count. The scheduler.go change removed the error handling branch, losing diagnostic signal about *why* enrichment stopped early. While the current caller only logs this context, future callers (monitoring, alerts, adaptive retry) lose structured error information.
findings.recommendation: Keep the (int, error) signature. Enrichment stopping early for bot protection is materially different from hitting the budget limit. Return fetcher.ErrChallenge when anti-bot triggers (line 87) and a new ErrEnrichmentAborted when consecutive failures abort (line 100). Let the scheduler decide whether to escalate these conditions (e.g., trigger circuit breaker, notify operators, switch proxy pools). The 3-line error check in scheduler.go is negligible cost compared to the loss of diagnostic signal.

findings.title: Removed proxy eviction on bot protection in Fetch, creating behavioral inconsistency
findings.description: The Fetch() method previously evicted proxies from the client pool when bot protection was detected (lines 166-168 in yad2.go, now removed). FetchItem never had this logic. This creates an asymmetry: listing-page bot challenges don't evict the proxy, but item-page bot challenges never did either. The clientPool exists specifically to manage proxy health, but the only eviction callsite (line 160 on generic errors) now misses the most actionable signal: bot protection. Proxy pools are useless if they don't evict proxies that get challenged.
findings.recommendation: Restore the eviction on line 166. If the goal is to avoid evicting proxies on transient challenges, add a challenge-attempt counter per proxy and evict only after N consecutive bot responses. Removing eviction entirely defeats the purpose of having a proxy pool with health tracking.

findings.title: countMissingKm function name no longer matches behavior
findings.description: The countMissingKm function (line 138) counts listings with Km <= 0, but the Enrich() method now fetches for missing Km *or* missing ImageURL *or* missing City (lines 53-57). The function name is misleading because it doesn't count all listings that *need* enrichment, only those missing mileage. It's used in log messages (lines 63, 88, 101) to report 'remaining' items, which undercounts the actual enrichment candidates.
findings.recommendation: Rename to countNeedsEnrichment and update the logic to count listings where (Km <= 0 || ImageURL == "" || City == ""). This accurately reflects what Enrich() considers 'remaining work'. The function is private and called only within enricher.go, so the rename is safe.

residual_risks.description: Scheduler loses ability to react to enrichment abort reasons (bot protection vs consecutive failures). If future requirements include adaptive backoff, proxy rotation, or circuit-breaking based on failure mode, the signal is lost and must be re-added.

Bot-challenged proxies are no longer evicted from the client pool. If a proxy gets permanently flagged by the site's anti-bot, it will remain in rotation indefinitely, causing persistent ErrChallenge until manual intervention or the pool restarts.
